newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks face testing time in budget aftermath.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks face testing time in budget aftermath.

text.p: The British stock market has confounded doom merchants who warned of a collapse, after last week's budget snatched away lucrative dividend tax credits for pension funds and companies.
But analysts say the market is still absorbing the impact of the first Labour budget in nearly two decades and it is too early to say whether stock vaulations are too high at current levels.
The FTSE 100 index defied gravity last week, shooting to new record highs in roller-coaster trade, in what sceptics called unjustified euphoria.

"The market's attitude to the budget in general has been rather sanguine. It seems investors are trying to disentangle what the budget's ultimate impact on the market will be," said David McBain, UK stock strategist with NatWest Markets.
"It's not as clear cut as one may think, and it probably will drip feed into the market over time," he added.
The abolition of the dividend tax credits was well flagged through a series of leaks ahead of the budget.

Nick Knight, stocks strategist at Nomura, said the reason the market had not fallen after the budget was either because its impact was already priced in given the leaks, or because the moves had not yet hit the market.
McBain said he expected to see more of a reaction to the move after August 4, when the abolition of dividend tax credits actually goes into effect.

The move implies valuations should be reduced by nine percent, SocGen strategist Andy Hartwill said. The chief mitigating factor was the cut in the corporate income tax rate to 31 percent from 33 percent, he said.
"The market's reaction to the budget was all wrong. It's crazy," said Hartwill, who looks for the FTSE 100 to drop to around 4,500 before ending the year around 4,600.
The FTSE is currently hovering around 4,800 after hitting a record 4,879.0 on July 4.

The effect of the abolition of the dividend tax credit, he said, was likely to increase. Other negative factors were the threat of higher interest rates, increased employment costs, pressure on corporate earnings and a strong currency.
But the market could take about three months to adjust for these factors, Hartwill added.
Yet, the current backdrop of historically high liquidity could limit the downside for UK equities, strategists said.

Perhaps the overriding factor supporting the UK stock market was its relative underperformance to other international markets, coupled with the sharp appreciation of sterling, which should draw in foreign investment, added NatWest's McBain.

Panmure Gordon economist Stuart Weatherby said he expected European funds, which remain underweight in UK equities and virtually unaffected by the removal of dividend tax credits, to be drawn in to the UK market since P/E ratios are still relatively cheap compared with French and German stocks.
